clinicalPearls: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis produces painful, recurrent, round or oval ulcers with a yellow-grey base and an erythematous halo
Ulcers characteristically affect non-keratinised, movable mucosa such as the labial and buccal mucosa, sparing the hard palate and attached gingiva
Minor aphthae are small and heal without scarring in one to two weeks, while major aphthae are larger, deeper, and can scar
Herpetiform ulcers are numerous tiny lesions that may coalesce, despite the name they are not caused by herpes virus
It is a clinical diagnosis of recurrent ulceration in an otherwise well patient, and lesions recur in the same tissue types
Precipitants include stress, local trauma, certain foods, hormonal changes, and cessation of smoking
Aphthous-like ulceration can be a marker of haematinic deficiency, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or Behcet disease
Management is largely symptomatic with topical agents to relieve pain and inflammation, alongside correcting any deficiency
reference.pathophysiology: The precise cause is not fully understood, but recurrent aphthous stomatitis is considered a T-cell mediated immune reaction directed at the oral epithelium, producing focal ulceration. A genetic predisposition is common, and episodes are triggered by factors such as local trauma, stress, hormonal fluctuation, and specific foods. Systemic contributors, including deficiencies of iron, folate, or vitamin B12, and gastrointestinal or systemic inflammatory conditions, can precipitate or worsen ulceration. The lesions represent localised epithelial destruction with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate that heals as the immune response subsides.
additionalDifferentials: Ulceration from coeliac or inflammatory bowel disease
Erosive lichen planus or immunobullous disease
Oral squamous cell carcinoma presenting as a non-healing ulcer
additionalInvestigations: Clinical history focusing on frequency, pattern, and triggers
Haematinics (iron studies, folate, vitamin B12) and full blood count
Coeliac serology when gastrointestinal features or deficiency present
Assessment for systemic features suggesting Behcet or inflammatory bowel disease
Biopsy of any solitary ulcer that fails to heal to exclude malignancy
redFlags: A single ulcer persisting beyond two to three weeks, which must be investigated to exclude oral cancer
Ulceration with systemic features such as genital ulcers or ocular inflammation suggesting Behcet disease
Severe or atypical ulceration pointing to underlying systemic or immunodeficiency disease
reference.prognosis: Most patients have self-limiting recurrent episodes that heal without scarring and can be controlled symptomatically, though major aphthae may scar and some cases reflect a treatable underlying systemic condition.
pitfalls: Dismissing a persistent solitary ulcer as aphthous when it may be malignant
Failing to screen for haematinic deficiency or coeliac disease in severe or new-onset cases
Confusing herpetiform aphthae with herpes simplex infection
Overlooking systemic disease such as Behcet when extra-oral features are present
management: Use topical corticosteroids (such as a betamethasone mouthwash, triamcinolone in dental paste or hydrocortisone mucoadhesive pellets) as first-line treatment to shorten episodes
Provide symptomatic relief with topical local anaesthetic, chlorhexidine or antiseptic mouthwash, and barrier or coating agents
Advise trigger avoidance: minimise oral trauma, switch to a sodium lauryl sulphate-free toothpaste, and avoid identified precipitant foods
Correct any underlying haematinic deficiency of iron, folate or vitamin B12
For severe or refractory ulceration, escalate to systemic therapy such as colchicine or a short course of systemic corticosteroids
Investigate and treat an underlying systemic cause such as coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or Behcet disease when features suggest it
Biopsy any solitary ulcer that fails to heal to exclude malignancy
